items.prompt: A frontend mock was written months ago. What does it reflect?
choices: The provider's response as it looks today, kept in sync automatically by the test runner
The provider's response as someone believed it looked when writing it
Only the fields the provider team marked as public
items.explanation: A mock is a frozen guess. It does not follow the provider unless something checks it.

items.prompt: In contract testing, who is the consumer?
choices: The side that serves the API to other callers
The shared service that stores contracts for both teams
The side that calls the API and relies on its response shape
items.explanation: The consumer is the caller, such as a frontend or another service.

items.prompt: In contract testing, who is the provider?
choices: The side that serves the API and must satisfy its contracts
The side that calls the API and renders its response onscreen
The tool that generates mocks
items.explanation: The provider serves the responses and owes each consumer its contract.

items.prompt: What is a contract in this unit?
choices: A legal agreement signed by both teams' managers and renewed every quarter
A mock server started by hand before tests
A record of the requests a consumer makes and the responses it expects
items.explanation: It is a concrete data record, not a legal document or a running server.

items.prompt: Why did the backend's own tests stay green after the rename?
choices: They check the backend against itself, and it was consistent
They are forbidden from reading any field names in other teams' code
They only run after the frontend deploys
items.explanation: A rename done everywhere inside the backend still looks correct from inside the backend.

items.prompt: Was hand-writing the mock a mistake?
choices: Yes, mocks should never appear in any test suite
No, mocks isolate tests; the gap is nothing keeps them accurate
Yes, the frontend should always call the live backend in every test run
items.explanation: The mock did its isolating job. Contract testing adds the missing accuracy check.

items.prompt: Which approach would catch the rename but is slow and flaky?
choices: A full end-to-end test with both real services running
A unit test of one pure helper function
A lint rule on the frontend's import order and file naming habits
items.explanation: End-to-end tests hit the real API, but need live environments.

items.prompt: What does consumer-driven mean?
choices: The provider writes one spec of every possible field
The broker decides which fields every caller is permitted to read
The consumer writes the contract from what it actually uses
items.explanation: Contract content comes from real consumer usage.

items.prompt: A team mocks a shipping API with fields `id` and `carrier`. The provider renames `carrier` to `carrierName`. Both teams' CI stays green. What is the underlying cause?
choices: The provider team skipped their own test suite before releasing the renamed field
The consumer's mock library contains a bug in how it parses fields
Nothing ever compares the consumer's mock with the real provider's response
Renaming a field always requires a version number bump to deploy
items.explanation: Each suite is consistent with its own side, so the mismatch is invisible to both.
items.reference:
Two green suites, one broken page
frontend tests run against: a hand-written mock (total)
backend tests run against: its own code (totalAmount)
the link between mock and real API: checked by nobody
Why: each side is consistent with itself, so the disagreement lives between them where no suite looks.
items.learnMore:
Why a mock alone drifts

A mock records what someone believed the provider returned on the day it was written. The provider keeps changing; the mock does not, and nothing compares the two.

Common mistake

Concluding that mocks are the problem. Mocks isolate tests well; the gap is only that nothing keeps them accurate.
items.reflection: Think of a note you copied from someone else, such as a phone number or a recipe. What would tell you it had gone out of date, and who would notice first?

items.prompt: A team says: we mock the provider, so we already have contract testing. What is the strongest objection?
choices: The hand-written mock is never checked against the real provider
Mocks are slower than a real call to the provider's API
Mocks cannot return JSON bodies with more than two fields
Contract testing requires the provider to expose a public URL for every environment
items.explanation: A contract is checked by the provider; a mock is only the consumer's belief.

The provider renames a field the consumer reads

Between the two sides, in a place neither suite checks

items.prompt: What format usually holds a contract?
choices: A compiled binary built by the provider's release pipeline
A data file, usually JSON, listing interactions
A spreadsheet maintained by a project manager
items.explanation: A contract is plain data that both sides can read.

items.prompt: Each interaction in a contract pairs what with what?
choices: A test name with its runtime in milliseconds
An exact request with the response shape expected
A provider version with the engineer who shipped it
items.explanation: Request in, expected response out.

items.prompt: How is a contract typically generated?
choices: By the provider team writing it from memory after every release meeting
By scanning production traffic logs each night
By running the consumer's own tests against a mock and recording them
items.explanation: It is a byproduct of a real consumer test.

items.prompt: No consumer reads a field. May the provider change it?
choices: Yes, if no contract mentions it
No, fields are permanent once shipped
Only after every consumer team approves in a meeting
items.explanation: The contracts tell the provider exactly what is pinned.

items.prompt: What is the provider's real obligation?
choices: Everything an abstract spec could ever list
Only the fields used by the newest consumer
The union of what its actual consumers use
items.explanation: It owes what is actually relied on.

items.prompt: What goes wrong with one abstract spec for all consumers?
choices: No field can be changed safely without checking each consumer by hand
Consumers can no longer send any requests to the provider once it ships
The spec cannot be written in JSON format
items.explanation: An abstract spec pins every listed field, whether anyone reads it or not.

items.prompt: A checks `id` and `status`; B also checks `totalAmount`. After a rename of `totalAmount`, whose verification fails?
choices: A's
B's
Both A's and B's
items.explanation: A never looked at the field, so A's contract is unaffected.

items.prompt: Is a recorded contract a hand-written guess?
choices: No, it is recorded from a real consumer test
Yes, the consumer types it from memory
Yes, the provider drafts it and consumers sign
items.explanation: That recording is what separates it from a hand-written mock.

items.prompt: Three consumers' contracts never mention a `metadata` field. The provider wants to drop it. What do the contracts tell the provider?
choices: It is unsafe until all three consumer teams meet and approve the change together
No contract pins it, so removal should keep all verifications passing
It is unsafe because abstract specs list every possible field
It is safe only if the broker marks it as deprecated first
items.explanation: Pinned fields are exactly those in some contract.
items.reference:
Who may a rename hurt?
field `id`: read by A and B, pinned by two contracts
field `totalAmount`: read by B only, pinned by B's contract
field `shippingAddress`: read by nobody, pinned by none
Why: the provider's real obligation is the union of what its actual consumers use, nothing more and nothing less.
items.learnMore:
Consumer-driven contracts

Each consumer records only the fields it reads. The provider can then see exactly which changes are safe: anything no contract mentions, and nothing a contract does.

Common mistake

Treating the contract as a complete spec of the API. It describes one consumer's usage, not everything the provider offers.
items.reflection: Picture a shared fridge in a flat. Which rules matter to each person, and how could the group learn which items someone depends on before throwing them out?

items.prompt: The provider adds a new `currency` field to responses. Contracts list only `id` and `totalAmount`. What happens to verification?
choices: It fails because the response now differs from the recorded body
It fails until every consumer re-records its contract
It passes only if the new field is added to the abstract spec
It still passes, since consumers asked only about their own fields
items.explanation: A subset match lets additions through.

choices: Nothing, since extra fields in a contract are always ignored
The consumer's own test fails at once and shows the problem
The provider is blocked from changing a field nobody needs
Provider verification crashes instead of reporting a failure

items.prompt: What does the consumer test talk to?
choices: The live production provider running in the cloud
The provider team's database
A mock provider built from the contract
items.explanation: The consumer side stays inside its own CI.

items.prompt: What does provider verification talk to?
choices: A mock of the consumer's page rendered in a browser for tests
The provider's real code, replaying recorded interactions
The consumer's production servers
items.explanation: It replays what the contract recorded against real code.

items.prompt: Does either half need a live network call between the services?
choices: Yes, the consumer half always does
No, both run at unit-test speed
Yes, the provider half always does
items.explanation: That is why they are cheap and not flaky.

items.prompt: Does provider verification need the frontend's JavaScript?
choices: Yes, it must import the whole frontend bundle and execute it
Yes, it must render the page once
No, only the recorded interactions and its own code
items.explanation: The contract carries everything the provider needs.

items.prompt: Why does this work across different tech stacks?
choices: The contract is plain data, and neither side runs the other's code
Both teams must use the same language and the same framework version
The broker translates all code between stacks
items.explanation: A data file has no language.

items.prompt: Which test catches a field-shape mismatch the same way on every run?
choices: A test that depends on live data timing
A manual check on release day
A contract test
items.explanation: Replaying recorded data is deterministic.

items.prompt: 4 consumers each need 3 scenarios checked end to end. How many e2e paths is that?
items.explanation: 4 times 3 is 12 paths.

items.prompt: What does the pyramid gain from contract testing?
choices: More slow tests at the top of the pyramid
Fewer slow cross-service tests, kept safe
No unit tests are needed any more
items.explanation: Contracts replace the shape-checking end-to-end tests.

items.prompt: A team swaps 6 end-to-end paths (2 consumers, 3 scenarios each) for contract verification. How many verifications does the provider run?
items.explanation: One verification per consumer, however many scenarios its contract records.
items.reference:
Two fast halves around one file
consumer test: talks to a mock built from the contract
contract file: the shared record both sides trust
provider verification: replays the file against real provider code
Why: neither half needs the other's code or a live network, so both run at unit-test speed.
items.learnMore:
Two-sided verification

The consumer records, the provider replays. Because the contract is plain data, the two teams can use different languages and run in separate pipelines.

Common mistake

Assuming the provider must run the consumer's code. It only needs the recorded interactions and its own implementation.
items.reflection: Think of two people translating a document who never meet. What shared artifact would let each check their half without the other in the room?

items.prompt: Which two things does provider verification need in CI?
choices: The consumer's source tree and a running consumer build
A live production database and the consumer's contract
The recorded contract and the provider's own code
A staging copy of the frontend and the provider's code
items.explanation: It never needs to execute the consumer.

items.prompt: Does a contract catch an auth flow that spans several calls?
choices: No, it checks one request and response at a time
Yes, it records every call in order and replays that order
Yes, but only for the first call
items.explanation: A contract has no model of call order.

items.prompt: Does a contract catch a race between two services?
choices: Yes, races always change a response body
Yes, the broker detects every race
No, contracts are stateless snapshots
items.explanation: Races need a sequence-aware test.

items.prompt: Does a contract catch a DNS misconfiguration?
choices: Yes, DNS details are part of every response body it records
No, verification never uses the real network path
Yes, but only on the first run
items.explanation: Verification calls the handler directly or via localhost.

items.prompt: What is worse than having no contract at all?
choices: A contract with only one interaction
A contract nobody verifies in CI
A contract written in JSON
items.explanation: It gives false confidence while catching nothing.

items.prompt: What makes a contract actually catch drift?
choices: The contract file existing in the repository
A reviewer reading it once a quarter
The verification step running on every build
items.explanation: The file records; the replay enforces.

items.prompt: What do contracts replace?
choices: End-to-end tests whose job was checking response shape
Every end-to-end test in the whole system, including auth flows
Unit tests of the provider's logic
items.explanation: Only shape-checking e2e tests become redundant.

items.prompt: How does provider verification reach the provider?
choices: It goes through the production load balancer
It uses the consumer's browser session
It calls the handler directly or via localhost
items.explanation: That is why network-layer faults are invisible to it.

items.prompt: Should a team delete all its end-to-end tests after adopting contracts?
choices: No, flows, ordering and infrastructure still need them
Yes, contracts cover everything they covered
Yes, but only the ones that run slowly
items.explanation: Contracts narrow the e2e suite, they do not remove it.

items.prompt: Contract verification is green, but in production a login works on the first call and the session is lost on the second. Why was it missed?
choices: The contract file used JSON, which cannot hold session data
The provider verification ran before the consumer test finished
Contracts check single request and response pairs, not call sequences
Contract testing only covers GET requests and nothing else
items.explanation: Sequence bugs need an integration or end-to-end test.
items.reference:
Inside and outside the contract's reach
inside: field renames, removed fields, changed values, status codes
outside: call ordering, session flows, timing between services
outside: DNS, TLS, load balancer setup, network partitions
Why: a contract is one request and response checked in isolation, and it is only as strong as the CI step that replays it.
items.learnMore:
Limits of contract testing

Contracts are stateless snapshots checked against code called directly or over localhost, so anything that depends on sequence or on the real network path needs another kind of test.

Common mistake

Deleting all end-to-end tests afterwards. Only the ones whose job was checking response shape are replaced.
items.reflection: Think of a smoke alarm. What kinds of danger does it cover, what kinds does it miss, and what happens if nobody ever tests its battery?

X is protected against renames but not against removed fields
items.explanation: Without the replay step the files enforce nothing.

items.prompt: What is a broker?
choices: A person who negotiates API changes
A shared service both CI pipelines publish to and query
A mock server for the consumer's tests
items.explanation: It is the shared registry for contracts and results.

items.prompt: What does can-i-deploy ask?
choices: Was this exact provider version verified against every contract in production?
Did most tests pass in the last week?
Has the consumer team approved in chat?
items.explanation: It is a precise per-version question.

items.prompt: A provider version satisfies 3 of 4 contracts. Does can-i-deploy pass?
choices: Yes, a majority is enough
Yes, if the failing one is small
No, all four must verify
items.explanation: One broken consumer is enough to block.

items.prompt: Why use a broker instead of passing contract files by hand?
choices: It makes the contracts shorter to read
It tracks which contracts each provider version was verified against
It removes the need for any verification
items.explanation: Tracking is what makes the deploy gate possible.

items.prompt: A consumer's contract was never verified against this build. What is the answer?
choices: Yes, it is probably fine
No, whatever the team feels about the risk
Yes, if no one complains
items.explanation: Unverified is not safe.

items.prompt: Four consumers use one provider. How many contracts must it satisfy?
choices: One at a time, in order
Only the most recent two
Four at the same time
items.explanation: Each consumer has its own contract.

items.prompt: Verification runs 4 times a day. What is the worst-case wait to catch a bad change?
choices: 6 hours
4 hours
24 hours
items.explanation: A day divided by 4 runs is 6 hours.

items.prompt: Must the provider team ask each consumer team before release?
choices: Yes, always, one team at a time
Yes, but only the mobile team
No, the broker already holds the CI results
items.explanation: That is what the central record is for.

items.prompt: Provider v7 is verified against the web and mobile contracts. The admin app's contract, in production, was never verified against v7. What does can-i-deploy say?
choices: Yes, two of three consumers are verified
No, an unverified contract counts as not safe
Yes, admin is an internal tool and needs no check
No, but only if the admin team files a complaint
items.explanation: Every contract in production must have a pass for this exact version.
items.reference:
One gate, every consumer
provider v7 vs web contract: verified
provider v7 vs mobile contract: verified
provider v7 vs admin contract: never verified, so no deploy
Why: the check is a conjunction over every consumer in production, because one broken consumer is broken for its users whatever the others show.
items.learnMore:
The broker and can-i-deploy

The broker stores contracts and records, per provider version, which contracts that version was verified against. Before release, the gate asks if every contract in production is covered by a pass.

Common mistake

Reading a majority of passes as good enough. A single failing or unverified contract blocks the deploy.

items.prompt: Implement `hasField(body, key)`: return true if `body` has its own property `key`.
items.explanation: A renamed field shows up as the old key being absent, so presence is the first thing to check.

items.prompt: Implement `sameStatus(expected, actual)`: return true if the two status codes are equal.
items.explanation: Status is compared first because it is one value with one right answer.

items.explanation: Only the contract's keys are walked, so extra keys on the actual side are never reported.

items.explanation: A changed value is a break even when the key is still present.

items.prompt: Implement `countInteractions(contract)`: return how many interactions the contract records.
items.explanation: A contract is a list of interactions, so its size is the list length.

items.prompt: Implement `failedDescriptions(results)`: given `{ description, ok }` items, return the descriptions of those where `ok` is false.

tests.expr: expect(failedDescriptions([{ description: "a", ok: true }, { description: "b", ok: false }])).toEqual(["b"])

items.explanation: Reporting which interaction failed, not only that something did, is what makes a failure actionable.

items.explanation: One failing interaction fails the whole verification.

items.explanation: Replaying a recorded request means working out which resource its path names.

items.prompt: Implement `verifyContract(interactions, getActual)`. Each interaction is `{ description, request, response: { status, body } }`; `getActual(request)` returns `{ status, body }`. An interaction passes when the status is equal and every field listed in the expected body is present and equal in the actual body. Extra actual fields are allowed. Return `{ passed, failures }` where `failures` lists the descriptions of failing interactions, in order.

tests.expr:
const ix = [{ description: "order 123", request: { path: "/orders/123" }, response: { status: 200, body: { id: "123", totalAmount: 4999 } } }];
expect(verifyContract(ix, () => ({ status: 200, body: { id: "123", totalAmount: 4999 } }))).toEqual({ passed: true, failures: [] })

const ix = [{ description: "order 123", request: { path: "/orders/123" }, response: { status: 200, body: { id: "123", totalAmount: 4999 } } }];
expect(verifyContract(ix, () => ({ status: 200, body: { id: "123", total: 4999 } }))).toEqual({ passed: false, failures: ["order 123"] })

const ix = [{ description: "order 123", request: { path: "/orders/123" }, response: { status: 200, body: { id: "123", totalAmount: 4999 } } }];
expect(verifyContract(ix, () => ({ status: 200, body: { id: "123", totalAmount: 4999, currency: "XXX" } })).passed).toBe(true)

const ix = [{ description: "missing order", request: { path: "/orders/9" }, response: { status: 404, body: null } }];
expect(verifyContract(ix, () => ({ status: 200, body: {} }))).toEqual({ passed: false, failures: ["missing order"] })

items.explanation: Status is compared exactly and the body by subset: every key the contract lists must match, while keys it never mentions are ignored. Missing bodies are treated as empty so the 404 case does not crash.
items.reference:
Comparing a response to a contract
status: must equal the contract's status
each listed body field: must be present and equal
extra fields the contract does not list: ignored
Why: this subset rule lets providers add fields safely while still catching renames, removals and changed values.
items.learnMore:
The verification rule

For each recorded interaction, compare status first, then every field the contract lists. Fields the contract never mentions are not checked, which is what leaves the provider free to add things.

Common mistake

Comparing whole bodies for equality. That rejects harmless additions and defeats consumer-driven contracts.

items.prompt: Implement `failingConsumers(contracts, getActual)`. Each contract is `{ consumer, interactions }` with interactions as `{ description, request, response: { status, body } }`; `getActual(request)` returns `{ status, body }`. Return the names of consumers with at least one failing interaction, in the given order. An interaction fails when the status differs or any field listed in the expected body is missing or different (extra actual fields are fine).

tests.expr:
const cs = [{ consumer: "web", interactions: [{ description: "d", request: {}, response: { status: 200, body: { a: 1 } } }] }, { consumer: "mobile", interactions: [{ description: "d", request: {}, response: { status: 200, body: { b: 2 } } }] }];
expect(failingConsumers(cs, () => ({ status: 200, body: { a: 1, c: 3 } }))).toEqual(["mobile"])

const cs = [{ consumer: "web", interactions: [{ description: "d", request: {}, response: { status: 200, body: { a: 1 } } }] }];
expect(failingConsumers(cs, () => ({ status: 200, body: { a: 1 } }))).toEqual([])

const cs = [{ consumer: "web", interactions: [{ description: "ok", request: { p: 1 }, response: { status: 200, body: { a: 1 } } }, { description: "bad", request: { p: 2 }, response: { status: 200, body: { a: 5 } } }] }];
expect(failingConsumers(cs, (r) => ({ status: 200, body: { a: r.p } }))).toEqual(["web"])

const cs = [{ consumer: "web", interactions: [{ description: "d", request: {}, response: { status: 404, body: null } }] }];
expect(failingConsumers(cs, () => ({ status: 200, body: {} }))).toEqual(["web"])

items.prompt: Implement `canIDeploy(version, consumers, results)`. `consumers` is an array of consumer names in production; `results` is an array of `{ version, consumer, passed }`. Return true only if every consumer has a result for this exact `version` with `passed` true. A consumer with no result for the version means false.

tests.expr: expect(canIDeploy("v7", ["web", "mobile"], [{ version: "v7", consumer: "web", passed: true }, { version: "v7", consumer: "mobile", passed: true }])).toBe(true)
expect(canIDeploy("v7", ["web", "mobile"], [{ version: "v7", consumer: "web", passed: true }, { version: "v7", consumer: "mobile", passed: false }])).toBe(false)

items.explanation: Every consumer in production must have a passing result for this exact version. A missing result is treated as a no, and a pass recorded for another version does not carry over.
